1.pericope_label: After these things, and the establishment thereof, Sennacherib king of Assyria came, and entered into Judah, and encamped against the fenced cities, and thought to win them for himself. And when Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib was come, and that he was purposed to fight against Jerusalem, He took counsel with his princes and his mighty men to stop the waters of the fountains which were without the city: and they did help him. So there was gathered much people together, who stopped all the fountains, and the brook that ran through the midst of the land, saying, Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find much water? Also he strengthened himself, and built up all the wall that was broken, and raised it up to the towers, and another wall without, and repaired Millo in the city of David, and made darts and shields in abundance. And he set captains of war over the people, and gathered them together to him in the street of the gate of the city, and spake comfortably to them, saying, Be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria, nor for all the multitude that is with him: for there be more with us than with him: With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the Lord our God to help us, and to fight our battles. And the people rested themselves upon the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch find the didactic cast of the narrative already in its opening, the chronicler dropping the dated notice of Kings for a loose connective, and note that the waterworks are narrated in neither Kings nor Isaiah though both confirm them elsewhere; the verb, they insist, means not to block but to conceal, covering the springs and leading their water into underground channels, and the stream so dried up is the Gihon. They record that the clause about the towers is obscure, since mounting them is meaningless and the causative leaves the sentence without an object, and they hold the account not inconsistent with the tribute recorded in Kings. Ellicott collects the Greek, Latin and Jewish forms of Sennacherib's name against the monumental Sin-ahi-iriba, quotes the royal inscription claiming forty-six strong cities of Hezekiah, explains the omission of the submission and tribute by the chronicler's purpose of relating a deliverance, reports Keil's further suggestion that the negotiations had no bearing on the issue and rejects the explanation of Thenius that the writer shrank from recording a forced sacrilege. On the building notice he prefers a different division of the Hebrew letters giving raised towers upon it, against the reading of Thenius, takes the outer wall for the one enclosing the lower city, glosses Millo as the rampart, traces the encouragement to Elisha and to Jeremiah, and cautions that only the substance of the speech is given.

Gill dates the invasion to the fourteenth year and describes what the opening formula covers, the reformation settled, the throne secure, the Philistines beaten and the Assyrian yoke thrown off; he reduces the closing exhortation to its contrast, weak mortal men on the one side and the Lord on the other.

Clarke says God did not permit this pious prince to be disturbed until the reformation he had begun was complete, states from Kings the tribute of three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold that emptied the treasury and stripped the house of the Lord, supplies the military sense of stopping the springs since a great army could not subsist in an arid country, and points to the crusaders of 1099 reduced to distress when the inhabitants stopped the wells against them; he traces the saying about the greater number on our side to Elisha. Wesley hears a warning in the opening formula rather than a reward, that a man may be squarely in the way of duty and still meet trouble, which God permits to try his confidence, and explains the waterworks in a clause, that the water was drawn by secret pipes into the city.
Henry ends the paragraph where Paul does, that if God is for us none can be against us, and that by the favour of God enemies are lost and friends gained.

debates.question: Why does this account omit the submission and tribute recorded in Kings?

positions.position: Because the chronicler means to relate a deliverance and omits whatever would weaken that impression
Because the negotiations had no bearing on the after-course and issue of the war
Because the writer was unwilling to mention a forced sacrilege, an explanation Ellicott rejects

debates.question: What does the clause about the wall and the towers mean?

positions.position: A different division of the Hebrew letters gives and raised towers upon it, which is probably correct
Keep the received text and read it as heightening the towers, since the wall already had them
The clause is simply obscure, mounting the towers being meaningless and the causative leaving no object

outliers.claim: Illustrates the stopping of the springs from the first crusade, when the people of Jerusalem stopped the wells in 1099 and reduced the besieging army to great necessity

9.pericope_label: After this did Sennacherib king of Assyria send his servants to Jerusalem, (but he himself laid siege against Lachish, and all his power with him,) unto Hezekiah king of Judah, and unto all Judah that were at Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith Sennacherib king of Assyria, Whereon do ye trust, that ye abide in the siege in Jerusalem? Doth not Hezekiah persuade you to give over yourselves to die by famine and by thirst, saying, The Lord our God shall deliver us out of the hand of the king of Assyria? Hath not the same Hezekiah taken away his high places and his altars, and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, saying, Ye shall worship before one altar, and burn incense upon it? Know ye not what I and my fathers have done unto all the people of other lands? were the gods of the nations of those lands any ways able to deliver their lands out of mine hand? Who was there among all the gods of those nations that my fathers utterly destroyed, that could deliver his people out of mine hand, that your God should be able to deliver you out of mine hand? Now therefore let not Hezekiah deceive you, nor persuade you on this manner, neither yet believe him: for no god of any nation or kingdom was able to deliver his people out of mine hand, and out of the hand of my fathers: how much less shall your God deliver you out of mine hand?

schools.summary: Ellicott suspects the ninth verse has lost a verb and that the word for army has dropped from the phrase about his power, which means strictly his dominion, and against the silence of the great inscription on the siege of Lachish he sets the British Museum relief with its legend that Sennacherib sat on a raised throne and caused the spoils of Lachish to pass before him. He states that these verses reproduce in brief the leading ideas of the longer speech in Kings, renders the opening as a double question, finds the idiom of sitting in distress in Jeremiah, notes that the coarse expression of the older account is here softened, and observes that the chronicler is even more emphatic than Kings in asserting the sole validity of the one altar. He adds Assyrian parallels throughout: Esarhaddon boasting that he cut off food and water, the life of their souls; the fondness of Assyrian kings for invoking their predecessors; and Assurbanipal carrying the gods and goddesses of Elam to Assyria and naming nineteen of them. He explains the reasoning of the taunt by the ancient view that strong nations have strong gods, and notes that some manuscripts and all the versions read the closing verb as singular. Keil and Delitzsch say only the main ideas of the speech are reported, remark that the same thought is much more coarsely expressed in Kings, and put the logic plainly, that gods reckoned mightier had failed, so what could a lesser do.

Gill places the embassy after the tribute had been paid and the invader withdrawn, names the Rabshakeh as chief speaker and recalls that the envoys had been asked to use Syriac, glosses the God of Jerusalem as the only living and true God worshipped in the temple there, and reduces the opening taunt to its question, on what power in heaven or on earth do you rely.

Clarke likewise makes the message a second and separate act, the silver and gold having been received and the army withdrawn before Rabshakeh was sent, and refers the reader to the fuller account in Kings.

Henry sorts the attack into two charges. Against the king it was an attempt to detach subjects from their allegiance by means unbecoming a crowned head, representing him as one who would deceive his people into ruin by famine and thirst, who had exposed them to divine displeasure by removing the high places and altars, and who held out against a force certain to destroy them. Against God it was impiety, setting the Maker of heaven and earth beside the dunghill gods of the nations, the work of men's hands, as though an infinite and eternal Spirit had no more wisdom or power than a stone or the stock of a tree, and arguing not merely how shall your God deliver you but how much less, as if this one were feebler than all the rest.

outliers.claim: Sets the silence of Sennacherib great inscription about the siege of Lachish against the bas-relief in the British Museum, whose legend describes the king enthroned while the spoils of Lachish pass before him

16.pericope_label: And his servants spake yet more against the Lord God, and against his servant Hezekiah. He wrote also letters to rail on the Lord God of Israel, and to speak against him, saying, As the gods of the nations of other lands have not delivered their people out of mine hand, so shall not the God of Hezekiah deliver his people out of mine hand. Then they cried with a loud voice in the Jews’ speech unto the people of Jerusalem that were on the wall, to affright them, and to trouble them; that they might take the city. And they spake against the God of Jerusalem, as against the gods of the people of the earth, which were the work of the hands of man. And for this cause Hezekiah the king, and the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz, prayed and cried to heaven. And the Lord sent an angel, which cut off all the mighty men of valour, and the leaders and captains in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned with shame of face to his own land. And when he was come into the house of his god, they that came forth of his own bowels slew him there with the sword. Thus the Lord saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib the king of Assyria, and from the hand of all other, and guided them on every side. And many brought gifts unto the Lord to Jerusalem, and presents to Hezekiah king of Judah: so that he was magnified in the sight of all nations from thenceforth.

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps pointing to the compression: the note that more was spoken shows no full report is intended, and the letters are frankly out of sequence, since they were sent after the first embassy failed, so that on a strict order the verse would follow the shouting rather than precede it; he treats it as a parenthesis and allows that abbreviation has its necessities. He notes that the Greek and Latin make the shouting the work of one speaker, identifies the stated purpose as the chronicler's own summary of the long speech in Kings, observes that this writer passes over the terms offered in order to fix on the blasphemy that brought the Assyrian down, supplies the number of the slain from Kings, renders the verb of destruction as caused to disappear, and reports Hitzig's suggestion that three psalms were composed by Isaiah to commemorate the deliverance. On the closing comment he judges the emendation gave them rest round about to be correct, citing the Greek and Latin and the chronicler's use of that phrase elsewhere, and thinks the word enemies has fallen out. Keil and Delitzsch defend the received text against exactly that conjecture, taking the verb to mean leading with care and so protecting and holding the supposed scribal slip improbable, and they observe that no number is given for the slain because the number did not matter, the point being that the host was annihilated.

Gill refers the reader to the fuller narratives, names the Rabshakeh as the chief speaker, glosses the God of Jerusalem as the only living and true God, infers that Isaiah must have prayed although no account says so, since the king had asked it and an answer came through him, and reports three views of the destroying angel, the Targum making it the Word of the Lord sending Gabriel, Josephus taking it for the pestilence, and others for the Samiel or poison wind of the east; he declines to choose, holding only that it came from God and did what had been foretold.

Clarke supplies the names of the parricides and of the god in whose house the king fell, and puts the motive of the gift-bringers drily, that they saw whose friend Hezekiah was and had no wish to make an enemy of such a man. Wesley gives the Jewish comment on the angel in fuller form, Gabriel again, the execution done by lightning, and the night the passover night, the very night the firstborn of Egypt died.

Henry closes the section on the note he struck at its opening, that by the favour of God enemies are lost and friends gained, and reads the presents brought to Hezekiah as the honour paid to one who was manifestly the particular care of Heaven.

debates.question: What was the angel that destroyed the Assyrian host?

positions.position: The Word of the Lord sending Gabriel, by lightning, on the passover night
The pestilence, according to Josephus
The Samiel, the poison wind of the east that kills multitudes at a stroke
Simply the angel of the Lord, the number of the slain being unstated because immaterial

debates.question: Is the closing phrase about guiding them round about sound?

positions.position: No: read gave them rest round about, with the Greek and Latin and the chronicler usage elsewhere
Yes: the verb means leading with care and so protecting, and the supposed scribal slip is improbable

outliers.claim: Reports Hitzig hypothesis that Psalms 46 to 48 were composed by Isaiah to commemorate the destruction of the Assyrian army, supported by the kinship between their language and the prophet own

24.pericope_label: In those days Hezekiah was sick to the death, and prayed unto the Lord: and he spake unto him, and he gave him a sign. But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up: therefore there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem. Notwithstanding Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord came not upon them in the days of Hezekiah.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the single verse epitomises two long chapters elsewhere, names the prophet as the mouth through which God spoke, identifies the sign as the shadow going back on the dial of Ahaz, and observes that the Hebrew puts the sign first for emphasis. On the pride he refers to the reception of the Babylonian embassy, notes the promise made in sickness to walk humbly and its breach after recovery, and identifies the wrath with the prophecy that the treasures would go to Babylon and some of the royal sons serve as eunuchs there; Judah and Jerusalem are included because they shared the confidence in an arm of flesh. He takes the humbling to be the recorded reply that the word spoken was good. Keil and Delitzsch call what survives here mere hints, note that the speaking and the giving have God for their common subject, locate the pride specifically in the display of the treasures and in an idle trust in the alliance and in his own resources, wonder whether a threat in Micah belongs with the wrath, and state plainly that the judgment was postponed rather than cancelled and fell only later in the Chaldean invasion.
Gill refers the sickness and the sign to the fuller accounts, and on the humbling admits the text does not say what form it took, guessing at sackcloth, fasting, prayer and confession of sin.

Clarke sends the reader to Kings for the sickness, describes the fault as a vain confidence that took pleasure in riches and showed them off to the Babylonian messengers, and describes the repentance as an inward motion, a man waking from sleep, grieved at his sin and deprecating the anger he had drawn. Wesley enumerates three things that turned the king's head, the prodigious victory over the Assyrians, the miraculous restoration from sickness, and the honour of an embassy from so great a king, and suspects the root of it was a notion that these had been given him for his piety and virtues.

Henry alone stresses that the illness looked certain to be fatal, and gives the sign as the sun going back ten degrees. He sharpens the fault into an epigram, that having destroyed the other idolatries the man began to idolize himself, and made the very favours he had received the food and fuel of his pride; he presses the principle that pride is a sin God hates particularly in his own people, that it drew wrath on David when he numbered the people, and that a heart-sin is to be repented of though nothing worse comes of it, adding that subjects may have to mourn for the sins of their rulers and that the citizens humbled themselves either knowing they had shared the fault or fearing they would share the punishment.

debates.question: What did the humbling of Hezekiah consist in?

positions.position: Unstated in the text; perhaps sackcloth, fasting, prayer and confession
An inward motion, waking from sleep, grieved at the sin and deprecating the wrath
The recorded reply to Isaiah that the word of the Lord was good

outliers.claim: Formulates the fault as self-idolatry, that having destroyed the other idolatries of the land the king began to idolize himself, and made the favours he had received the food and fuel of his pride

27.pericope_label: And Hezekiah had exceeding much riches and honour: and he made himself treasuries for silver, and for gold, and for precious stones, and for spices, and for shields, and for all manner of pleasant jewels; Storehouses also for the increase of corn, and wine, and oil; and stalls for all manner of beasts, and cotes for flocks. Moreover he provided him cities, and possessions of flocks and herds in abundance: for God had given him substance very much. This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the wealth in a series with David, Solomon and Jehoshaphat, take the shields as standing for weapons in general and connect the collection with the armoury mentioned in Kings, derive the word for storehouses from a root meaning to heap up and treat it as a transposition, and do the same with the word for stalls, which occurs here in a form found nowhere else. On the cities they deny the word can bear its usual sense in this context and offer either watch-towers or dwellings for herdsmen, noting that the term covers any enclosed place from a tower to a walled town; on the waterworks they describe the upper outlet closed in and the water carried by a subterranean channel westwards into the city of David, and discuss the contracted form of the verb. Ellicott compares the same three predecessors, recalls the golden shields of Solomon and the brazen ones of Rehoboam, renders the last item as vessels of desire, lists the cognate forms of the word for stalls and suspects a copyist has transposed the last two words of the verse, since the Hebrew says flocks for folds where the Greek and Latin read folds for the flocks. He settles the disputed word as watch-towers or forts for the protection of flocks and herds, and points out that Kings refers to the same waterworks in its own closing summary while this writer supplies further particulars.

Gill supplies the sources of the wealth, the spoil of the Assyrian camp and the presents sent afterwards by neighbouring nations, keeps the ordinary sense of cities and explains them as the places where the storehouses and stalls stood with lodgings for those who managed them, mentioning a reading in some copies of the Vulgate that makes them six, and on the waterworks cites the identification of Gihon with Siloam and quotes Maundrell measurement of the pool outside the Bethlehem gate, a hundred and six paces by sixty-seven, lined with wall and plaster and well stored with water when he saw it.

Clarke renders the last item of the treasuries as desirable vessels or utensils, and speaks plainly of canals cut to bring the water of Gihon from the west side of Jerusalem to the west side of the city of David. Wesley takes the verb about the cities as repairing, fortifying and beautifying them for the honour and safety of the kingdom, and distinguishes the two streams of the rivulet, the upper gathered into what Isaiah calls the upper pool and the lower into another, saying it was the upper that was diverted and piped into the city, a work of great art and labour.

Henry gathers the paragraph under the honour God gave the man while he lived, notes that the diversion of the stream was undertaken when the Assyrian came and that the new gathering of the water served the city better than the old pool, and remarks that he prospered in all his works because the works were good ones.

debates.question: What are the cities that Hezekiah provided for himself?

positions.position: Watch-towers or forts for the protection of the flocks and herds
Or else simply dwelling-places for herds and herdsmen
Ordinary towns, where the storehouses and stalls stood with lodgings for their keepers
Existing towns repaired, fortified and beautified for the honour and safety of the kingdom

outliers.claim: Quotes Maundrell measurement of the pool of Gihon outside the Bethlehem gate, a hundred and six paces long by sixty-seven broad, lined with wall and plaster and well stored with water at the time of his visit

31.pericope_label: Howbeit in the business of the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, who sent unto him to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land, God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart. Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and his goodness, behold, they are written in the vision of Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, and in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel. And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David: and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honour at his death. And Manasseh his son reigned in his stead.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch insist the connective never carries an adversative sense, adopt Bertheau rendering and accordingly, and explain that it reconciles an episode which was no part of the king's good fortune with the statement that he prospered in everything; they say the permission was given not to ruin but to humble him, take the vision of Isaiah for the book of that prophet prophecies and so a work distinct from the chronicle of the kings, read the burial phrase as on the height of the graves of the sons of David, and guess the hereditary vault was full. Ellicott paraphrases the same connective as and thus, while things stood so prosperously, names Merodach-baladan as the sender and calls the princes of Babylon another vague rhetorical plural, observes that the errand of enquiry appears in no parallel account but fits what the monuments show of Babylon as the home of divination, notes that the verb for trying is the ordinary one for tempting and that the clause about knowing must mean bringing to light what was latent, since the Searcher of hearts knew the outcome already. He deletes the conjunction so as to make the vision a section within the book of the kings, prefers the ascent for the burial phrase, supports the crowding of the tombs by noting that the next three kings were not buried there either, and holds that these closing statements, appearing in no canonical parallel, argue for a source besides Kings.

Gill rejects two explanations of the embassy errand before giving his own, dismissing the Targum notion that they came to see the tables of stone in the ark and Grotius view that they asked about the destruction of the Assyrians, and holding it was the retreat of the sun they wanted explained, the Chaldeans being much given to astrology; he glosses the king goodness as his acts of piety and liberality.

Clarke draws his lesson from the Targum gentler version, in which the Word of the Lord merely permits the showing and the king does not suffer for it, and adds that to know one's own weakness is the beginning of watchfulness, since he who does not know where his weakness lies is not likely to know where his strength lies; he reads the burial phrase simply as respect paid to the best king since David. Wesley allows either the destruction of the Assyrians or the going back of the sun as the wonder enquired after, and ends on the debt owed to those who have been eminently useful, to honour them at their death when they are beyond the reach of flattery.

Henry takes both explanations of the errand and supplies a motive for each, since the Assyrians were their enemies and their fall worth rejoicing over, while the sun was their god and they would honour a man their god had honoured; on the leaving alone he gives the sharpest formulation in the chapter, that God left him to be proud of his wealth in order to keep him from being proud of his holiness.

debates.question: What did the Babylonian envoys come to enquire about?

positions.position: The retreat of the sun, the Chaldeans being much given to astrology; not the tables of stone, nor the fall of the Assyrians
Either the destruction of the Assyrians or the going back of the sun
The sign, an errand unmentioned elsewhere but fitting Babylon as the home of divination and portent-reading
The two tables of stone in the ark, with the broken ones, according to the Targum

debates.question: What is the vision of Isaiah cited as a source?

positions.position: The book of Isaiah prophecies, a work distinct from the chronicle of the kings
A section within the book of the kings of Judah and Israel, the conjunction being deleted

debates.question: What does the chiefest of the sepulchres mean?

positions.position: The height of the graves of the sons of David, higher ground used because the vault was full
The ascent, the way up to the royal tombs
Respect paid to the best king since David

outliers.claim: Explains the clause about God knowing what was in Hezekiah heart by the analogy of a chemist subjecting an imperfectly known substance to various combinations in order to ascertain its nature, since the Searcher of hearts knew the issue beforehand
